title: Kashmir, Spiti and Sikkim: Planning India’s Three Great Mountain Trips
metaDescription: How to plan trips to Kashmir, Spiti Valley and Sikkim — seasons, permits, altitude, routes and costs for India’s three most rewarding mountain regions.
excerpt: Three Himalayan regions, three completely different trips. The mistake is treating them as interchangeable.
author: Trypinn Team
content:
India's Himalaya is not one destination. Kashmir, Spiti and Sikkim sit within the same mountain range and offer three fundamentally different trips — different seasons, different terrain, different cultures, different logistics.

Choosing between them properly, rather than picking whichever came up first, makes a large difference to whether the trip works.

## Kashmir: The Accessible One

**What it is:** A broad green valley ringed by mountains, with lakes, meadows, Mughal gardens and a distinctive culture. The most comfortable of the three — you can do Kashmir without camping, without altitude sickness, and without a four-wheel drive.

**When to go**
- **April to May** — tulip season in Srinagar, blossom in the valley, and the most beautiful window
- **June to August** — warm, green, peak domestic season, and the time for the high meadows and treks
- **September to October** — autumn colour, chinar trees turning, fewer visitors, excellent weather
- **December to February** — snow, Gulmarg skiing, and a completely different, quieter trip

**The route**
- **Srinagar** — Dal Lake and a houseboat stay, the Mughal gardens, the old city and its wooden mosques, Shankaracharya Hill
- **Gulmarg** — a meadow at 2,650m with the Gondola cable car running to 3,980m. Skiing in winter, walking in summer
- **Pahalgam** — a river valley, the base for the Kolahoi glacier trek and Aru and Betaab valleys
- **Sonamarg** — the gateway to Ladakh and to the Thajiwas glacier
- **The Great Lakes Trek** — a week-long high-altitude circuit past a series of alpine lakes, and one of India's finest treks

**Practicalities:** Fly to Srinagar. No permits required for the main valley. Check current travel advisories and local conditions before booking, and follow local guidance while you are there. Mobile connectivity can be restricted at times. Kashmiri hospitality is genuinely remarkable and the food — wazwan, rogan josh, the bread culture — is a reason to go on its own.

![India travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1552978534-9d01e1f91517?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Spiti: The Hard One

**What it is:** A high-altitude cold desert, culturally and visually Tibetan, at 3,000 to 4,500 metres. Barren, enormous, and utterly different from the green Himalaya people picture. The most physically demanding of the three and, for many travellers, the most memorable.

**When to go**
- **June to September** — the only period both routes into the valley are reliably open
- **Mid-May to June** — the Manali route usually opens with the Kunzum Pass
- **October** — beautiful, cold, and the Manali route starts closing
- **November to April** — accessible only via Shimla and Kinnaur, and only to Kaza. Winter Spiti is a serious expedition with temperatures well below -20°C, and is genuinely spectacular for those equipped for it

**The two routes, and why it matters**
- **Via Shimla and Kinnaur** — longer, gradual, and it gains altitude slowly. This is the route that lets you acclimatise properly
- **Via Manali and the Kunzum Pass** — shorter and much more dramatic, and it takes you from 2,000m to 4,500m in a day, which is the single most common cause of altitude sickness in Spiti

**The strong recommendation: go in via Shimla, come out via Manali.** This gives you gradual acclimatisation on the way up and a spectacular exit.

**The route**
- **Kalpa and Kinnaur** — apple orchards beneath Kinner Kailash
- **Nako** — a village around a small lake at 3,600m
- **Tabo** — a thousand-year-old monastery with extraordinary murals
- **Dhankar** — a monastery on a crumbling spur above the confluence
- **Kaza** — the main town and base
- **Key Monastery** — the iconic stacked monastery, and the image most people have of Spiti
- **Kibber, Komic, Hikkim and Langza** — among the highest villages in the world, with a fossil-rich valley and the world's highest post office
- **Chandratal** — a high-altitude lake, camping only, accessible in a short summer window
- **Pin Valley** — the quieter side valley, and snow leopard country in winter

**Altitude is the real constraint.** Spend two nights below 3,500m before going higher, ascend gradually, hydrate heavily, avoid alcohol for the first days, and know the symptoms of acute mountain sickness. Descend if they appear — this is not negotiable.

![India travel](https://images.unsplash.com/photo-1465919292275-c60ba49da6ae?fm=webp&w=1200&q=60)

## Sikkim: The Green One

**What it is:** A small state between Nepal and Bhutan, densely forested, culturally Buddhist with Nepali and Lepcha influences, and dominated by Kangchenjunga — the world's third-highest mountain — visible from much of the state.

**When to go**
- **March to May** — rhododendron season. The best window, and the reason many people go
- **October to early December** — the clearest mountain views of the year
- **June to September** — monsoon, heavy rain, landslides, and roads regularly blocked. Avoid
- **Winter** — clear and cold, with snow in the north

**The route**
- **Gangtok** — the capital, pleasant and well organised, with MG Marg and Rumtek Monastery nearby
- **Tsomgo Lake and Nathu La** — a high lake and a pass on the Chinese border, requiring permits
- **North Sikkim — Lachen and Lachung** — the Yumthang Valley for rhododendrons, Gurudongmar Lake at 5,400m, and Zero Point. Requires permits and a registered operator
- **West Sikkim — Pelling and Yuksom** — the best Kangchenjunga views, Pemayangtse Monastery, and Yuksom as the trailhead for the Goecha La trek
- **The Goecha La trek** — eight to ten days to a pass with a close view of Kangchenjunga. One of India's great treks
- **Silk Route and Zuluk** — a series of switchbacks on the old trade route to Tibet, in East Sikkim

**Permits:** Foreign nationals need an Inner Line Permit for Sikkim, easily obtained, plus additional protected area permits for north Sikkim and the border areas. Indian nationals need permits for the restricted areas. **North Sikkim must be booked through a registered operator** — you cannot do it independently. Build this into the plan rather than discovering it in Gangtok.

## Which One Should You Choose?

**Choose Kashmir if** you want comfort, beauty, culture and food without altitude or hardship, and you want it accessible to a mixed group including older travellers or children.

**Choose Spiti if** you want the high Himalaya at its most severe and otherworldly, you can handle altitude, and you have at least ten days — Spiti done in a week is a road trip with altitude sickness attached.

**Choose Sikkim if** you want mountains and forest together, rhododendrons or clear Kangchenjunga views, and a shorter, easier trip than Spiti with better infrastructure.

## Shared Practicalities

- **Book vehicles and drivers** rather than self-driving. Mountain roads in all three regions are demanding, and a local driver is inexpensive and dramatically safer
- **Cash.** ATMs are scarce and frequently empty outside main towns. Carry more than you think you need
- **Connectivity.** Patchy to absent. Download offline maps. In Spiti, only certain networks work at all
- **Weather closes roads.** Build buffer days into every mountain itinerary, especially before an international flight. A landslide is not a rare event
- **Altitude.** Relevant in Spiti and north Sikkim especially. Acclimatise, and take symptoms seriously
- **Accommodation** is simple outside the main towns — homestays and guesthouses rather than hotels. This is part of the appeal, and worth setting expectations about

Mountain trips are where loose planning genuinely costs you, because the constraints are real: permits that need arranging in advance, passes that are seasonally closed, altitude profiles that must ascend gradually, and weather that will take a day from you. Laying the route out with the altitude and the permit requirements visible — and with buffer days written in rather than assumed — is the planning that makes these trips work. **Trypinn** keeps the whole group looking at the same version of it.
